chunk_findings.detail: The change turns a deliberately function-local import into a module-level one: `from ...config import Config, _is_code_tree` in `gates/defs.py`, `from ..config import _is_code_tree` in `macros.py` and `companions.py`. The original code fetched `_is_code_tree` lazily inside the loading function precisely because `ddflow.config` imports the service modules (directly, or via `services/__init__`) and defines `_is_code_tree` later in the module than that import point. That is exactly why `gates/defs.py` could already import `Config` eagerly (it is defined early) but had to defer `_is_code_tree`, and why `companions.py` had no module-level `ddflow.config` import at all. With the new eager import, a fresh interpreter that reaches a service module before `ddflow.config` finishes executing — e.g. `python -c 'import ddflow.services.macros'`, or any `ddflow` command whose import graph pulls in macros/companions/gates — executes `from ..config import _is_code_tree` against a partially initialized `ddflow.config` and raises `ImportError: cannot import name '_is_code_tree' from partially initialized module 'ddflow.config' (most likely due to a circular import)`. That aborts every command, including the out-of-tree invocation the fix is supposed to repair, so the regression test must be run in a fresh process (as the task requires) to avoid masking it behind an already-imported `ddflow.config`.

The original line `if led["done"]["files_known"] and globs and not conflicts(sorted(landed), globs):` relied on Python's left-to-right short-circuiting: when `led["done"]["files_known"]` was false, or when `globs` was falsy (e.g. `None`/absent, which is exactly why the `and globs` term exists in the same expression), it never touched `landed` or `globs`. The retained `and globs` guard in the very next line is now unreachable for that input, which is the tell that the guard was defeated by hoisting the match out of the condition. chunk_findings.detail: The new expression `inside = any(path_in_glob(p, g) for p in landed for g in globs)` is evaluated *unconditionally*, before the `if led["done"]["files_known"] and globs and not inside:` guard. The original line `if led["done"]["files_known"] and globs and not conflicts(sorted(landed), globs):` relied on Python's left-to-right short-circuiting: when `led["done"]["files_known"]` was false, or when `globs` was falsy (e.g. `None`/absent, which is exactly why the `and globs` term exists in the same expression), it never touched `landed` or `globs`. After the change, the generator always iterates both. Given an input where the ledger's `files_known` is false (or a verification run with no declared globs) and `globs` is `None`, the old code fell through and appended nothing; the new line executes `for g in globs` on `None` and raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable` at line 221, aborting the verification instead of skipping the note. The retained `and globs` guard in the very next line is now unreachable for that input, which is the tell that the guard was defeated by hoisting the match out of the condition. (Same class of regression if `landed` is `None` when `files_known` is false, since `for p in landed` also runs unconditionally.)

That is exactly where the pre-existing code computes `base = fx.base ...` (the value this change replaces) and the test list, and no other line between `rec = st.bugs.get(bug_id)` and `fx = ...` exists that could produce it. Because an assignment anywhere in the function makes `module_tests` a local for the whole frame, the fast path raises `UnboundLocalError: local variable 'module_tests' referenced before assignment`. Demonstrated input: a fix task whose landing was recorded (`fx.landed_before` and `fx.landed_after` both non-empty — the ordinary post-merge state this change targets), then `ddflow complete <fix> --regression-test tests/test_importer_validators.py`; the branch is taken (`tree=repo`, `after=...`) and the crash happens on argument evaluation, before `verify_regression_test` is even entered, so the regression check fails with a traceback instead of returning `verified`/`could-not-run`. The guard placement is deliberate (it must precede the `if tree is None` early return because the worktree is gone after a merge), so the fix needs the test list bound above the fast path (or passed in) rather than below it.

chunk_findings.detail: `_case(repo)` returns the fix task's worktree (`wt`), and a git worktree cannot have `main` checked out while the primary checkout already has it, so `wt` is on the fix branch (or detached). The `pass_pipeline`/merge path records the pre-fix tree from the sha the task branched from (per the intent: "merge-base recorded at claim/worktree creation, or the first parent of the merge commit"), and that sha predates the `git add -A` + `git commit -qm always` that this test performs at lines ~32–35. So `tests/test_always.py` does not exist in the pre-fix tree at all, and the scenario the test claims to cover ("a test that passes [on the pre-fix tree]") cannot occur. Concretely, when the check runs `pytest tests/test_always.py::test_always` against the recorded base it gets a "file not found / no tests ran" error: if `_verify_regression` reads any non-zero exit as "fails on the pre-fix tree", the regression is accepted and `assert res.exit == 3` fails (res.exit would be OK); if instead it is treated as could-not-run, the assertion only passes because the reason string happens to contain "pre-fix tree", i.e. the test is vacuous and never exercises the pre-fix-pass refusal it is named for. To actually create a test that passes before the landing, `tests/test_always.py` must be committed on `main` *before* the fix branch/worktree is created, not added inside the fix worktree.

chunk_findings.detail: `_case(repo)` returns the fix task's worktree (`wt`), and a git worktree cannot have `main` checked out while the primary checkout already has it, so `wt` is on the fix branch (or detached). The `pass_pipeline`/merge path records the pre-fix tree from the sha the task branched from (per the intent: "merge-base recorded at claim/worktree creation, or the first parent of the merge commit"), and that sha predates the `git add -A` + `git commit -qm always` that this test performs at lines ~32–35. So `tests/test_always.py` does not exist in the pre-fix tree at all, and the scenario the test claims to cover ("a test that passes [on the pre-fix tree]") cannot occur. Concretely, when the check runs `pytest tests/test_always.py::test_always` against the recorded base it gets a "file not found / no tests ran" error: if `_verify_regression` reads any non-zero exit as "fails on the pre-fix tree", the regression is accepted and `assert res.exit == 3` fails (res.exit would be OK); if instead it is treated as could-not-run, the assertion only passes because the reason string happens to contain "pre-fix tree", i.e. the test is vacuous and never exercises the pre-fix-pass refusal it is named for. chunk_findings.detail: `test_a_call_that_hangs_is_cut_off_and_retried` runs `_run(tmp_path, "hang ok", call_timeout=3)`, which exports `MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT=3` for the whole process. That bound therefore also covers the second, non-hang call: the `ok` branch (`touch "$FAKE_DIR/listed"; echo "Successfully published"; exit 0`). Under the exact environment described in B6797d49e48 (host load ~160-200, fake publisher/curl calls exceeding 1 s), the `ok` retry can itself exceed 3 s, get killed as a hang, and be retried. The plan string only has two tokens ("hang", "ok"), so the third invocation exhausts the plan (the token selector matches nothing, the fake still appends to `$FAKE_DIR/publishes`) and the run ends with `publishes == 3` (or a non-zero exit from the unhandled branch), so `assert r["publishes"] == 2` fails. That is precisely the flake the change claims to eliminate, and it contradicts the change's own comment that "only the hang case asks for a short one" — the plan it uses pairs the hang with a call that is expected to return at once and should therefore run under the generous timeout. Setting the hang timeout to 3 only widens a margin that the bug report says was ~1 s under load, rather than removing the coupling between the hang timeout and the normal retry call.

chunk_findings.detail: `_met` short-circuits `dep_status` for any non-`removed`, non-`DONE` phase whose non-abandoned tasks are all `DONE`, returning `True`. That is exactly the "roadmap judges met with its own rule" divergence the bug is about, just narrowed to one case. Concrete input: `road_log()` with `P2` left un-closed and `T4` marked done (`g.done("T4", _ts(3))`), and `P3` waiting on `P2`. With the old code `waits_on` called `dep_status(state, "P2", cfg)`, which reports not-met because `P2` itself has not completed, so `P3` rendered under `## Later`. The removed test `test_a_phase_whose_tasks_are_done_but_which_is_not_closed_still_blocks` pinned precisely that behaviour and its docstring states "`next` waits for the phase itself to complete (its own pipeline), not just its tasks"; with the new `_met` that same input returns `True` and `P3` moves to `## Next`, so the roadmap once again disagrees with `ddflow next` for this input — i.e. B58010c24b3 is reintroduced rather than fixed, and the guard test that prevented the regression is deleted in the same diff. (The base docstring even asserted "the lanes and `ddflow next` agree (B58010c24b3)"; the rewritten docstring now openly concedes the exception, but an exception for a phase that is genuinely unfinished is a disagreement, not a representational nuance.) Note also that the phase's own lane under the stated lane rules ("DONE when its own state says so") is still not `DONE` in this scenario, so the comment "The lanes count such a phase DONE" is not what the lane logic does for the example above.

chunk_findings.detail: The change does not add a regression test that fails on the unfixed code; it edits the existing test so that it passes on both versions. The added line `g.add("item.completed", "P2", {"kind": "phase"}, _ts(3))` closes P2 before the assertion. On the pre-fix code, `_met` only takes its all-tasks-done shortcut when `it.state != DONE` (the `it.kind == "phase" and it.state != DONE` guard); once P2 is closed that guard is false, so `_met` falls through to `return dep_status(state, dep, cfg)[0]` — the exact call the fixed `waits_on` makes. Running this test against the pre-fix tree therefore passes, which contradicts the stated requirement ("write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"). chunk_findings.detail: The bug this fix addresses is described as a check-to-removal race: onboard "can delete a tree that an agent claimed *between its check and the removal*." That wording states the unfixed onboard *does* perform a check before removing; the defect is that the check and removal are not atomic (no log lock). This test performs no interleaving: it claims T1 first (`run_cli(repo, "claim", "T1", agent="worker")`) and only then calls `ON.apply(repo, [str(tree)])`. With the lease already present before `apply` runs, any check onboard already performs — even outside the lock — observes the lease and skips the removal, so the final `assert tree.exists()` holds on the *unfixed* code too. The test therefore does not fail on the current code as the task requires ("watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"), and it cannot distinguish the fix's central contribution (running `dispose_tree` under the log lock / atomic re-check) from the pre-existing non-atomic check. To actually regress this bug it would have to force the claim into the window between onboard's check and its removal (e.g. by interposing the claim before the removal call), which this test never does. If onboard in fact had no lease check at all, the bug would be a missing check rather than the described race, and then the fix's lock to describe would be untested regardless.

chunk_findings.detail: The change drops *every* `rubber_duck`/`critic` failure whenever `gate is None`, not just review-finding failures. The stated requirement was to keep failures that indicate saturation — "timeouts, unavailable reviewers, infrastructure errors" — and remove only review-finding failures. `_outcome(ev)`/`_gate(ev)` carry no failure reason (the new code only sees `g in PR.REVIEW_GATES`), so a review gate that failed because the reviewer timed out or the vLLM server was unavailable is now silently skipped, exactly like a reviewer that returned findings. Concrete input: a wave where 6 of 12 chunk reviews time out under load yields 6 failed `critic` outcomes; `_failure_rate(..., gate=None)` `continue`s on all six, so `gate_failure_rate`/`gate_failure_ratio` stay at zero and below their `low` mark, and `flowcontrol` keeps stepping the parallel ceiling upward while the reviewer/pipeline is genuinely saturated. The signal that exists to detect reviewer overload now cannot see it. The fix needs to key on the failure kind (timeout/unavailable vs. findings) rather than the gate name, or turn the ratio off by default as the requirement allowed, instead of asserting every review-gate failure is a finding.

chunk_findings.detail: The bug this fix addresses is described as a check-to-removal race: onboard "can delete a tree that an agent claimed *between its check and the removal*." That wording states the unfixed onboard *does* perform a check before removing; the defect is that the check and removal are not atomic (no log lock). This test performs no interleaving: it claims T1 first (`run_cli(repo, "claim", "T1", agent="worker")`) and only then calls `ON.apply(repo, [str(tree)])`. With the lease already present before `apply` runs, any check onboard already performs — even outside the lock — observes the lease and skips the removal, so the final `assert tree.exists()` holds on the *unfixed* code too. The test therefore does not fail on the current code as the task requires ("watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"), and it cannot distinguish the fix's central contribution (running `dispose_tree` under the log lock / atomic re-check) from the pre-existing non-atomic check. To actually regress this bug it would have to force the claim into the window between onboard's check and its removal (e.g. by interposing the claim before the removal call), which this test never does. If onboard in fact had no lease check at all, the bug would be a missing check rather than the described race, and then the fix's lock to describe would be untested regardless.

chunk_findings.detail: The new test asserts a *removal* behavior (`assert tree.exists()`) for an adopted tree, but whether that tree is removed is decided entirely by `_held(repo, cfg, log, path, item.branch)` and the surrounding `if held: return ...` / `W.remove(...)`, none of which are changed by this diff — they appear only as context lines. The only edited production lines are the `EventLog(...)` constructor arguments and the outcome string. Neither can change whether an adopted item's tree is removed, because the adoption check is inside the unchanged `_held` call. Consequently the test cannot be the required regression test: with the diff reverted, `ON.apply` takes the identical code path for this input, so the test either passed before the change too (if `_held` already honoured adoption) or still fails after it (if `_held` does not, in which case the fix is incomplete and CI is red). This diff contains no `dispose_tree` helper, no change to `api/lifecycle/merge.py`, `services/flow.py`, or `services/cleanup.py`, and only edits `onboard.py`. Therefore, if the report's premise about `cleanup` is correct, the defect it describes (after `cleanup` disposes a tree, the event log gets no `worktree.removed`, leaving `item.worktree` pointing at a deleted path) is entirely unaddressed by this change. At minimum the change does not do what its own description says it does.

chunk_findings.detail: The diff only swaps the agent id used to construct one `EventLog`. It does not implement the fix the intent claims: nothing adds the log lock, the post-check claim re-check, or the `worktree.removed` logging around onboard's removal, and `cleanup.py` is not touched at all. Given the bug description ("onboard also removes with force and without the log lock, so it can delete a tree that an agent claimed between its check and the removal"), the race is still live in this change: release tree T, invoke onboard on T, and have another process claim/lease T in the window between onboard's existence check and its force removal — onboard still deletes T, leaving the claimant with a lease pointing at a deleted worktree. The changed line cannot affect that interleaving. Likewise the stated stale-fold symptom for cleanup (`cleanup.py:322` never logs `worktree.removed`) is untouched, so a tree removed by `ddflow cleanup` still leaves `fold`'s `item.worktree` pointing at the removed path. chunk_findings.detail: The fixture injects `"gate_failure_ratio": 1.6`, but the bug report this test is derived from states the low mark for that signal is 1.5. So 1.6 is *above* the low mark, i.e. an active "reduce the limit" value (which is why it can be the signal that holds the limit), not "its neutral band" as the docstring claims. The reported incident is precisely the harder case: the ratio hovered at 1.2–1.6 with the mark at 1.5, i.e. mostly **below** the mark (1.2–1.4), where the signal blocks growth (holds the limit) without ever triggering a decrease of its own, so a "latest decision" that only remembers the last signal that *caused a decrease* still names the null `reviewer_latency_ratio`. Given the fixture as written, an implementation that attributes `limited_by` only to signals that actively lowered the limit passes `d.limited_by == "gate_failure_ratio"` here, while the observed symptom (status says "limited by reviewer latency ratio" with a null ratio) reappears for any sample where `gate_failure_ratio` sits below 1.5. To reproduce the incident, the 120-sample block should use a value below the low mark (e.g. 1.2–1.4), not 1.6.

chunk_findings.detail: The fixture injects `"gate_failure_ratio": 1.6`, but the bug report this test is derived from states the low mark for that signal is 1.5. So 1.6 is *above* the low mark, i.e. an active "reduce the limit" value (which is why it can be the signal that holds the limit), not "its neutral band" as the docstring claims. The reported incident is precisely the harder case: the ratio hovered at 1.2–1.6 with the mark at 1.5, i.e. mostly **below** the mark (1.2–1.4), where the signal blocks growth (holds the limit) without ever triggering a decrease of its own, so a "latest decision" that only remembers the last signal that *caused a decrease* still names the null `reviewer_latency_ratio`. Given the fixture as written, an implementation that attributes `limited_by` only to signals that actively lowered the limit passes `d.limited_by == "gate_failure_ratio"` here, while the observed symptom (status says "limited by reviewer latency ratio" with a null ratio) reappears for any sample where `gate_failure_ratio` sits below 1.5. To reproduce the incident, the 120-sample block should use a value below the low mark (e.g. 1.2–1.4), not 1.6.

With the patched code the fallback still selects `gate_failure_ratio` (the change only adds the helper call; the fallback path that names over-low signals is unchanged), so `limited_by == "gate_failure_ratio"` and growth is still held, exactly the condition the bug says must not hold ("failed review gates mean the reviewer found issues, not that capacity is short"). The change is cosmetic: it only relabels the reason. The new test itself encodes this: `assert _after_a_decrease(None, 1.6).limited_by == "gate_failure_ratio"` asserts that a review-finding ratio above the 1.5 low mark is the limiter, i.e. it pins the unfixed behavior as expected.

chunk_findings.detail: The bug this fix addresses is described as a check-to-removal race: onboard "can delete a tree that an agent claimed *between its check and the removal*." That wording states the unfixed onboard *does* perform a check before removing; the defect is that the check and removal are not atomic (no log lock). This test performs no interleaving: it claims T1 first (`run_cli(repo, "claim", "T1", agent="worker")`) and only then calls `ON.apply(repo, [str(tree)])`. With the lease already present before `apply` runs, any check onboard already performs — even outside the lock — observes the lease and skips the removal, so the final `assert tree.exists()` holds on the *unfixed* code too. The test therefore does not fail on the current code as the task requires ("watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"), and it cannot distinguish the fix's central contribution (running `dispose_tree` under the log lock / atomic re-check) from the pre-existing non-atomic check. To actually regress this bug it would have to force the claim into the window between onboard's check and its removal (e.g. by interposing the claim before the removal call), which this test never does. If onboard in fact had no lease check at all, the bug would be a missing check rather than the described race, and then the fix's lock to describe would be untested regardless.

chunk_findings.detail: The two sides of the comparison are now quoted differently. The changed-path set is read with `git status --porcelain -z`, which emits pathnames *verbatim* (no C-quoting at all), while the `diff` text is read with only `core.quotepath=false`. That setting only stops git from octal-escaping bytes with the high bit set; git *always* C-quotes backslash, double-quote and control characters, even with `core.quotepath=false`. So for a path containing `\`, `"`, or a control char the two representations no longer match, and `missing = [p for p in changed if p not in diff]` reports it as missing. Concretely: a tracked file named `a"b` (one double-quote) that is modified yields `path = 'a"b'` from `_status_paths`, but `capture_diff`'s output contains `a\"b` (git renders `diff --git "a/a\"b" "b/a\"b"`); `'a"b'` is not a substring, so `diff_covers_everything` returns `(False, ['a"b'])` even though the diff fully covers it. Same for a file named `a\b` (raw status `a\b` vs diff `a\\b`) and for tab/newline in a name. This is a regression rather than a pre-existing gap: before the change, status was read with default quoting and `strip('"')`, so both sides carried the same escapes (e.g. status `"a\"b"` → `a\"b`, which *is* in the default-quoted diff), and the old first-character bug did not affect quoted names because the eaten character was the opening quote. The fix only closes the mismatch for high-bit (non-ASCII) bytes while opening it for these always-quoted bytes.

chunk_findings.detail: The new failure test `then <= 0` conflates "the string could not be parsed" with "the timestamp is at or before 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z". The old code parsed the epoch instant successfully (`datetime.strptime("1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z", "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%fZ").timestamp() == 0.0`) and returned a finite age: `_age_s("1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z", now=1_790_000_000.0)` used to be `1_790_000_000.0`, and `_age_s("1969-12-31T23:59:59.000000Z", now=1_790_000_000.0)` used to be `1_790_000_000.0 + 1`; both now return `float("inf")`. That contradicts the function's own new docstring ("infinite when `ts` is not a timestamp") for inputs that *are* timestamps, and it only occurs because `epoch` apparently uses 0/negative as its parse-failure marker, so a legitimate pre-epoch value is indistinguishable from garbage. Practical impact is small (session records are modern), but any caller/test that treats `0.0`-valued timestamps as valid now sees "infinitely old"; if `epoch` instead signals failure with exactly `0.0`, the guard should be `then == 0.0` (or the sentinel should be checked via a distinct "parsed" result) rather than `then <= 0`.

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the `then <= 0` guard with `then == 0.0`, treating 0.0 as `epoch`'s sentinel for "not a timestamp" while (correctly) letting negative values through as real pre-1970 timestamps. But `epoch` derives its value from the parsed instant, so the valid timestamp `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` (and its microsecond form `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z`) also produces exactly `0.0`. That collides with the sentinel: `S._age_s("1970-01-01T00:00:00Z", now=THEN)` returns `float("inf")` instead of `THEN`, i.e. a perfectly valid timestamp is still reported as infinitely old — the same failure mode the bug describes. The newly added regression test probes only the second *before* the epoch (`1969-12-31T23:59:59Z`), so the boundary itself is untested and the sentinel ambiguity survives. Either `epoch` needs to signal "unparseable" out-of-band (e.g. `None`/raising), or `_age_s` must distinguish parse failure from a legitimate 0.0 epoch value.

chunk_findings.detail: `ts.replace("Z", "+00:00")` only attaches a timezone when the string actually ends in `Z`. For any value without a UTC designator — exactly the "imported or hand-edited records" this commit says it is fixing — `fromisoformat` produces a *timezone-naive* `datetime`, and `datetime.timestamp()` on a naive value uses the **host's local timezone** (platform `mktime`). So `_age_s("2026-10-06T10:00:00", now=NOW)` returns `NOW - 1746000000` on `TZ=Asia/Kolkata` (naive 10:00 read as 04:30 UTC → age overstated by 19800s) but `NOW - 1759744800` on a UTC CI/production host — the same stored record yields a different age depending on the machine, and DST transitions make the mapping ambiguous. The pre-change code called the shared `epoch` reader, whose accepted forms all carry a UTC designator (the very reason it returned 0.0/inf for `...:00Z` in this bug), so a Z-less value was rejected as "not a timestamp" rather than silently reinterpreted through the process timezone. If Z-less values are meant to be treated as UTC (which the rest of the log format assumes), naive results must be normalized (`dt.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)`) or rejected; if they are not valid inputs, the function should still not silently depend on the host timezone.

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard `if then <= 0: return float("inf")` conflates a parse failure with a valid Unix timestamp at or before the epoch. The old implementation parsed the microsecond form successfully and returned `now - 0.0`; the new code makes it infinite. chunk_findings.detail: `epoch()` returns `0.0` both for "not a timestamp" and for the legitimate Unix epoch, so the new equality sentinel `then == 0.0` still reports an infinitely old age for a valid timestamp — and `_age_s`'s own contract is "infinite when `ts` is **not** a timestamp". Concretely, `S._age_s("1970-01-01T00:00:00Z", now=THEN)` computes `then = 0.0`, the guard fires, and the function returns `float("inf")` instead of the true age `THEN`. The change deliberately taught the function that pre-1970 values are real (the added `test_a_timestamp_before_1970_has_a_real_age` asserts `1969-12-31T23:59:59Z` → `THEN + 1`), but stops exactly one second short of the boundary it claims to handle: `1969-12-31T23:59:59Z` is finite while `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` is infinite, an off-by-one-second discontinuity at the sentinel. The pre-existing test only covers genuinely unparseable strings (`"yesterday"`, `""`), so it does not pin down the sentinel and does not catch this. A sentinel that cannot collide with a real value (e.g. `epoch()` returning `None` for parse failure, or a separate "is a timestamp" predicate) is needed; otherwise the fix leaves the original bug class—"valid timestamp treated as infinitely old"—partially unaddressed at exactly the epoch.

chunk_findings.detail: For a record whose timestamp has no `Z`/offset (e.g. a hand-edited or imported record `"2026-10-06T10:00:00"`, or one written by a UTC clock that omits the suffix), `datetime.fromisoformat(...)` returns a naive datetime and `then = ....timestamp()` interprets it in the machine's local zone. On `TZ=Asia/Tokyo` the intended UTC instant is read 9 h early, so `_age_s` returns an age 9 h too large and a recent session can be pruned prematurely; on `TZ=America/New_York` it is read 4–5 h late and the session is treated as younger than it is, so it lingers. The pre-existing test and the new regression test only exercise the `Z` forms, so a CI box running `TZ=UTC` will never observe the discrepancy. The intended fix (routing through the shared reader, which normalizes to UTC) avoids this; the `try/except` also does not cover the `OverflowError`/`OSError` that `mktime`-based resolution of out-of-range naive dates raises on some platforms.
